exam: Define bicornuate uterus and its embryological basis. — Incomplete fusion of the Müllerian ducts resulting in a deep fundal cleft and two uterine horns with a single cervix.

What key history questions should you ask a woman with suspected uterine anomaly? — Number and timing of miscarriages, preterm births, malpresentations, infertility, menstrual abnormalities, and any renal or urinary symptoms.
Describe the bedside pelvic exam findings that suggest a bicornuate uterus. — Bimanual exam may reveal a midline fundal indentation; cervix appears single; uterine size may feel asymmetric.

How does 2‑D transabdominal ultrasound differentiate bicornuate from septate uterus? — Look for external fundal indentation ≥1 cm (bicornuate) versus smooth external contour (septate); internal septum thickness also assessed.
Why is MRI not essential for diagnosis in low‑resource settings? — A clear fundal indentation on good‑quality 2‑D scan meets diagnostic criteria; MRI adds little extra information.
What renal anomaly is most commonly associated and why must it be screened? — Unilateral renal agenesis; important for surgical planning and to avoid missed renal dysfunction.

When is Strassman metroplasty indicated and what are its main risks? — Indicated after ≥3 recurrent losses or preterm births with desire for term pregnancy; risks include hemorrhage, infection, adhesion formation, and uterine rupture in later pregnancy.

Why is hysteroscopic septum resection inappropriate for bicornuate uterus? — The defect is external (fundal) not an internal septum; resection would not correct the anatomy and may cause uterine rupture.

What antenatal monitoring is recommended if surgery is not performed? — Serial ultrasounds for fetal growth, cervical length measurement, and careful assessment of presentation; plan elective CS if malpresentation persists.

Explain how the presence of HIV might affect management of a pregnant woman with bicornuate uterus. — HIV may increase infection risk post‑surgery; prioritize antiretroviral therapy, consider prophylactic antibiotics, and ensure safe delivery planning.

What is the recommended mode of delivery for a term pregnancy with breech presentation in a bicornuate uterus? — Elective cesarean section is recommended due to high risk of obstructed labour and uterine rupture.

How would you counsel an asymptomatic woman incidentally found to have a bicornuate uterus? — Explain low baseline risk, advise on early ultrasound in future pregnancies, discuss signs of preterm labour, and reassure that most deliver vaginally if no complications.
What bedside test cannot reliably differentiate bicornuate from septate uterus? — Bimanual palpation alone; external contour cannot be felt accurately, imaging is required.
List three confounding factors that can mask the diagnosis on ultrasound. — Obesity, uterine fibroids, and a full bladder causing poor acoustic windows.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused obstetric‑gynaecologic history and a systematic pelvic exam can raise suspicion for a bicornuate uterus and rule out other causes of recurrent loss or malpresentation.

t.b: Is there a palpable midline depression >1 cm? Positive: suggests bicornuate uterus; negative does not exclude septate uterus.
Feel for two distinct uterine horns with a single cervix. Positive: supports bicornuate uterus; cannot assess depth of fundal cleft.
Identify a single cervical os. Positive: rules out didelphic uterus; does not differentiate septate from bicornuate.

t.a: Transabdominal scan at bedside (if portable US available)
t.b: Look for a midline fundal indentation on a sagittal view. Positive: suggests bicornuate uterus; limited resolution may miss shallow clefts.

b: 2‑D transabdominal ultrasound – first line; shows external fundal indentation and separate uterine horns.
3‑D ultrasound – gold standard in low‑resource centres with access; measures fundal depth and confirms single cervix.
MRI pelvis – definitive when ultrasound equivocal; demonstrates external contour and internal septum.
Renal ultrasound – screens for unilateral renal agenesis or ectopic kidney.
Hysterosalpingography (HSG) – evaluates cavity shape; will show a single cavity with a deep fundal cleft in bicornuate uterus.
sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Imaging is the cornerstone; each modality answers a specific anatomic question and has a fallback when unavailable.

t.b: Does the fundal cleft measure ≥1 cm depth? Yes = bicornuate uterus; <1 cm suggests septate or normal.
Shows two uterine horns with a single endometrial cavity; confirms bicornuate uterus; if not available, rely on 2‑D + clinical correlation.

t.a: MRI – T2 weighted sagittal and coronal images
t.b: External fundal indentation ≥1 cm with two separate horns confirms bicornuate uterus; also rules out septal thickness.

t.a: Renal ultrasound – presence of both kidneys
t.b: Detects unilateral renal agenesis (common association). If absent, arrange CT urography if MRI not possible.
Shows a single endometrial cavity with a deep fundal cleft; cannot assess external contour, so must be combined with US or MRI.

b: U3 (ESHRE/ESGE) – bicornuate uterus: external fundal indentation ≥1 cm, two uterine horns, single cervix.
Severity graded by depth of fundal indentation: shallow (1–2 cm) vs deep (>2 cm).
Presence of associated renal agenesis upstages risk for surgical planning.
Obstetric history (≥2 miscarriages, preterm birth, malpresentation) adds clinical severity.
sections.p: Classification follows the ESHRE/ESGE system (U3) and the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) categories.
Other Müllerian anomalies can mimic a bicornuate uterus on imaging; key discriminators are external contour and cervical anatomy.

t.b: Normal external fundal contour, internal fibrous septum dividing cavity. Separate by checking fundal indentation on 3‑D US or MRI; hysteroscopic resection is treatment.
Two separate uterine cavities, two cervices, often double vagina. Identify by speculum exam (two cervical os) and imaging showing two distinct uterine bodies.
Mild fundal indentation <1 cm, single cavity. Differentiated by measuring depth; usually benign, no surgical correction needed.

b: 1. Confirm diagnosis with bedside 2‑D ultrasound; document fundal indentation ≥1 cm and single cervix.
2. Counsel patient on reproductive risks, reassure if asymptomatic, and arrange baseline renal ultrasound to rule out renal agenesis.
3. For recurrent miscarriage or preterm labour, refer to a centre with expertise for Strassman metroplasty; otherwise continue expectant management.
4. Initiate antenatal surveillance early: serial growth scans, cervical length measurement, and weekly fetal presentation checks after 28 weeks.
5. Plan delivery: schedule elective cesarean section for breech, transverse lie, or failed trial of labour; otherwise allow vaginal delivery if head engagement is confirmed.
6. Escalate to tertiary centre if uterine rupture suspected, uncontrolled bleeding, or inability to monitor cervical length.
sections.p: A structured approach ensures safe care from initial assessment through definitive therapy and timely referral, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Progesterone (vaginal micronized) – reduces preterm birth risk; watch for vaginal irritation and rare allergic reaction; discontinue if severe irritation develops.
Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) – accelerate fetal lung maturity; avoid repeated courses within 2 weeks; monitor maternal glucose if diabetic.
Tocolytics (nifedipine) – relax uterine smooth muscle; monitor for hypotension, tachycardia, and avoid in severe cardiac disease.
Antibiotic prophylaxis for preterm premature rupture (ampicillin + erythromycin) – prevent infection; watch for rash and Clostridioides difficile; avoid if known severe allergy.
Iron supplementation – correct anemia; monitor for constipation and dark stools; avoid excess in hemochromatosis.
sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Medication choices focus on preventing preterm birth and managing complications; awareness of adverse effects avoids iatrogenic harm.

b: Uterine rupture – sudden abdominal pain, loss of fetal station, abnormal heart rate; immediate transfer for emergency laparotomy.
Severe preterm labour (<34 weeks) despite tocolysis – call tertiary obstetric unit for possible rescue steroids and advanced neonatal care.
Placental abruption – painful bleeding, uterine tenderness, fetal distress; urgent cesarean section if viable fetus.
Infection after metroplasty – fever, uterine tenderness, leukocytosis; start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics and refer to surgical team.
Persistent malpresentation at term – if breech or transverse lie persists, schedule cesarean section; avoid trial of vaginal delivery.
sections.p: Recognising obstetric and surgical complications early allows prompt referral and reduces maternal‑fetal morbidity.

b: HIV – increased risk of opportunistic uterine infections; CD4 count guides timing of surgery; avoid live vaccines in neonate.
Tuberculosis – pelvic TB can mimic uterine anomaly on imaging; obtain GeneXpert if chronic pelvic pain; treat TB before elective surgery.
Malnutrition – low albumin impairs wound healing after metroplasty; provide nutritional support before operative intervention.
Pregnancy – physiological uterine enlargement may obscure fundal cleft; use trans‑vaginal probe for better resolution.
Diabetes – higher infection risk and steroid‑induced hyperglycaemia; monitor glucose closely when giving betamethasone.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort) – can induce hepatic enzymes, reducing progesterone levels; advise cessation.
Alcohol – impairs fetal growth and may worsen preterm risk; counsel abstinence.
Renal or liver failure – adjust drug dosing (e.g., avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics); avoid metformin if severe renal impairment.
sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions can mask symptoms, alter test accuracy, or modify therapeutic choices.

b: Children – bicornuate uterus rarely diagnosed before menarche; use pelvic ultrasound only if symptomatic (e.g., dysmenorrhoea). Surgical correction postponed until after puberty.
Pregnancy – prioritize fetal monitoring, cervical length surveillance, and early delivery planning; avoid elective vaginal delivery if presentation uncertain.
Elderly women – rare presentation; assess for uterine atrophy and increased surgical risk; consider conservative management.
People with HIV – ensure viral suppression before any elective surgery; prophylactic antibiotics may be needed.
Low‑resource settings – rely on high‑quality 2‑D ultrasound with external fundal contour assessment; if MRI unavailable, use trans‑abdominal scan with a full bladder to accentuate indentation.
sections.p: Tailored strategies are required for vulnerable populations and resource‑limited environments.

ai.title: Bicornuate Uterus
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: A bicornuate uterus is a congenital uterine malformation where the uterine cavity is partially divided by a deep fundal cleft. It can cause reproductive complications but often remains asymptomatic.

b: Partial fundal cleft >1 cm on imaging
Single cervix, two distinct uterine horns
Often discovered incidentally on ultrasound or during infertility work‑up
sections.p: A bicornuate uterus results from incomplete fusion of the Müllerian ducts during embryogenesis, producing two uterine horns with a single cervix. Prevalence is 0.1‑0.4 % in the general population and higher among women with infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss.

b: Class U3: bicornuate uterus – external fundal indentation ≥1 cm
Distinguish from septate uterus (no external indentation)
Associated anomalies: renal agenesis, vaginal septum (Müllerian duct spectrum)
sections.p: Understanding the anatomy helps predict obstetric risks and guide management. The defect is classified as a Class U3 anomaly in the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) system.

b: First‑trimester miscarriage up to 30 % higher
Preterm birth risk 2‑3 times greater
Higher incidence of breech or transverse lie
sections.p: Most women are asymptomatic, but the malformation can lead to miscarriage, preterm labour, malpresentation, and intra‑uterine growth restriction. In low‑resource settings, limited imaging may delay diagnosis, increasing obstetric morbidity.

t.b: Is there a fundal cleft and how many cavities? – Shows a deep fundal indentation; if >1 cm suggests bicornuate uterus.
Can the external contour be visualised and cervical canal assessed? – Confirms two horns with a single cervical canal; differentiates from septate uterus.
What is the precise uterine anatomy? – Gold standard for delineating fundal depth and associated renal anomalies.
Are there concurrent renal anomalies? – Detects unilateral renal agenesis, common in Müllerian duct anomalies.

Metropolitan centres: Strassman metroplasty (open) for women with recurrent loss and desire for term pregnancy
Cesarean section recommended for breech or transverse lie in the third trimester
If surgery not feasible, close antenatal monitoring for growth, cervical length, and presentation
sections.p: Treatment is individualized. Asymptomatic women need counselling only. Symptomatic or obstetric complications may require surgical or obstetric interventions.

b: Septate uterus – normal external fundus, internal septum; managed surgically by hysteroscopic resection
Didelphic uterus – two separate cervices and vaginas; requires different surgical approach
2‑D ultrasound may underestimate fundal depth, mistaking a septate uterus for bicornuate
Absence of renal imaging can miss associated anomalies that affect surgical planning
